q: Do you know how many eyes a spider has?
Why do ladybirds have spots?
Can you guess how many times a bee flaps its wings in one second?
Do you know what a butterfly tastes food with?
a: Most spiders have eight eyes! Still, many see badly and feel the world mostly with their legs.
Red with spots tells birds: careful, I taste awful! So birds leave ladybirds alone.
More than two hundred times a second! That is why you hear the buzz.
Its feet! A butterfly tastes a flower as soon as it lands on it.

q: Do you know what happens to an astronaut's tear in space?
How many sunrises a day do astronauts on the space station see?
Do you know why space is completely silent?
Can you guess how many Earths would fit inside Jupiter?
a: It does not run down! Without gravity it stays by the eye like a little ball of water.
About sixteen! The station flies around the Earth in about an hour and a half.
Sound needs air to travel. Space has no air, so you would not hear even a big bang.
More than a thousand! Jupiter is the biggest planet in our solar system.

q: On which planet is a day longer than a whole year?
Do you know what colour a sunset on Mars is?
Can you guess which planet would float in water?
Do you know where in space it may rain diamonds?
a: On Venus! It turns around itself more slowly than it goes around the Sun.
Blue! The Martian sky is pinkish by day, but it turns blue around the setting Sun.
Saturn! For its size it is so light that it would float in a giant bathtub.
Scientists think diamonds may fall deep inside Neptune and Uranus!

q: Do you know which real animal is called a dragon?
Can you guess which lizard can run on water?
Do you know which little dragon really flies?
Which animals lived in the time of the dinosaurs and still live today?
a: The Komodo dragon! It is the biggest lizard in the world, up to three metres long.
The basilisk! It runs on the water so fast that it has no time to sink.
The flying dragon! This small lizard spreads the skin on its sides like wings and glides from tree to tree.
Crocodiles! Their ancestors lived alongside the dinosaurs.

q: Do you know how a baby bird gets out of its egg?
Can you guess which egg is the biggest in the world?
Do you know how a chick inside a closed egg can breathe?
Do you know which mammal lays eggs?
a: It has a tiny sharp bump on its beak, the egg tooth. It scratches the shell until it breaks through.
The ostrich egg! It is about as big as twenty hen eggs.
The shell has thousands of tiny holes that let air through.
The platypus! It is a mammal, but its babies hatch from eggs.

q: Do you know how many times a glass bottle can be recycled?
Can you guess what a new park bench can be made of?
Do you know why iron rusts?
Do you know how a big magnet can lift a car?
a: Again and again! Glass can be melted into a new bottle forever.
Old plastic bottles and caps! Recycling turns them into boards for benches.
When water and air touch iron for a long time, it gets covered with brown rust.
Junkyards have electromagnets that lift a whole car. When the power goes off, they let it go.

q: Do you know why gears have teeth?
Can you guess how many parts a bicycle has?
Do you know what a spring does in a watch?
Do you know what is inside a battery?
a: The teeth fit into each other, so when one gear turns, the other turns too.
About a thousand, if you count every screw, ball and chain link!
A wound-up spring slowly unwinds and that moves the hands.
Materials that react together and make electricity. When they are used up, the battery is flat.

q: Do you know what color a raindrop is?
Can you guess where a rainbow comes from?
Do you know why the air smells nice after a storm?
Do you know why you hear thunder after the lightning?
a: None! It is clear, we just draw it blue.
Sunlight goes through raindrops and splits into colors.
Rain lets out the smell of soil and plants, and lightning makes a little fresh ozone.
Light is much faster than sound, so you see the flash before you hear the thunder.

q: Do you know what makes a good password?
Can you guess how long people have used locks?
Do you know what a secret code is?
Do you know why you never tell anyone your password?
a: Long and hard to guess, for example three words that have nothing to do with each other.
Thousands of years! The ancient Egyptians had wooden locks with pins.
A message written so that only someone who knows the key can read it.
Whoever knows it can open your things. Only your parents may know it.

q: Do you know how a robot vacuum finds its way?
Can you guess where most robots work?
Do you know if a robot can feel a touch?
Do you know who made up the word robot?
a: It has sensors that feel walls and stairs, and some draw a map of the home.
In factories! They build cars, pack parcels and never get tired.
Some can! Sensitive sensors in their fingers let them gently hold even an egg.
The Czech writer Karel Čapek, about a hundred years ago.

intro: Together we will learn to type with all ten fingers.
Put your index fingers on the little bumps of F and J. That's home.
Let's start on the Training Meadow!
world1: The meadow is full of curious little visitors.
Type the word on a leaf and Piko fans it back with his fan.
When a leaf gets past, it is a goal and everybody cheers.
invitation: Look what {piko} found in the grass!
Your fingers are ready for a rocket flight.
world2: Your typing rhythm drives the rocket.
Push sleepy asteroids out of the way with a soft energy beam.
landing: The control tower says: landing clearance granted!
We are landing on a magical new planet.
world3: Build stepping stones across the swamp and choose paths at the signs.
Careful typing matters more than speed here.
force: You found something amazing: the Force!
Now you can move things gently, just by typing.
The dragons in the next valley need help.
world4: Space rocks are falling into the Dragon Valley.
Every word makes a shield bubble for a baby dragon.
The rocks just bounce away, nobody gets hurt.
egg: The dragons are safe and happy.
As a thank you, they give you a magical Dragon Egg!
world5: Oh! The egg starts to wiggle and roll down the hill.
Help it jump over rocks and stumps.
Watch out for a friendly mole!
hatched: A tiny baby dragon looks at you. You have a new friend!
Now you can go on rescue missions and help more dragons.
world6: Piko walks past an old junkyard. What is that beeping?
Someone is beeping sadly under a pile of old things.
Type a word and a soft magnet lifts the junk off the pile.
friends: A small rusty robot climbs out of the pile.
He wants to say thank you, but he can only beep: Beep beep!
He gives you a tiny gear. His name is Bolt, and now you are friends!
world7: Bolt wants to go home, but he is missing some parts.
Gears, bolts and springs ride along the conveyor belt.
Type a part's word and Piko tosses it into the basket.
legs: Done! Bolt has new long legs.
And a bright new yellow antenna on his head.
Now he can walk the long way home.
world8: Oh no, it starts to rain!
Robots must not get wet, or they rust.
Type the word on a raindrop and Piko's umbrella catches it.
raincoat: The rain stopped and a rainbow shines over the town.
Bolt gets a yellow raincoat and Piko a new umbrella.
Now no rain can hurt them.
world9: The way home leads through Robot City.
All doors are locked and the panels show passwords.
Type a password and the door opens with a chime.
key: Bolt found the key card to his home.
world10: Bolt's home is dark and all the robots are asleep.
Type a word and a lamp switches on.
The helper robots wake up and wave hello.
home: Bolt's family is so happy he is home.
They thank you, {name}, for helping Bolt.
Now you can repair little robots on rescue missions too.

about.title: About PikoTyper
about.intro: PikoTyper is a free, peaceful game that teaches children to type with all ten fingers. Together with a companion they travel through worlds full of adventures. Nothing bad ever happens: obstacles are pushed away or helped, never destroyed.
privacy: No tracking, no cookies, no analytics.
All progress is stored only in this browser; you can export it as a file.
Works offline after the first visit.
how: Keys are learned one by one, starting from the home row (F and J).
Every key has its finger; the on-screen keyboard and hands show which one.
Accuracy comes first; speed is only shown as a personal trend.
Weak keys appear more often, and short breaks keep sessions healthy.
about.credits: Open source under the MIT license. Fonts: Lexend, Atkinson Hyperlegible and OpenDyslexic (SIL Open Font License).

tips.sit-straight: Sit up straight and lean your back on the chair.
tips.feet-floor: Keep your feet flat on the floor or on a footrest.
tips.elbows-close: Keep your elbows near your body, not flying out.
tips.right-angles: Bend your elbows and knees at about a right angle.
tips.sit-higher: Sitting too low? Put a cushion under you.
tips.screen-distance: Keep the screen about an arm's length away.
tips.screen-height: Put the screen at eye level so your neck stays relaxed.
tips.relax-shoulders: Drop your shoulders, breathe out and relax your hands.
tips.wrists-float: Let your wrists float lightly, not bent.
tips.no-palms: Don't lean on your palms, keep your hands light.
tips.soft-touch: Press keys softly, no need to bang.
tips.thumbs-rest: Let your thumbs hover over the space bar.
tips.fj-bumps: Feel the bumps on F and J, your index fingers rest there.
tips.home-row: Home is the middle row: A S D F and J K L.
tips.return-home: After every letter, send your finger back home.
tips.one-finger: Every letter has its own finger, always the same one.
tips.index-two: Your index fingers do the most, two columns each.
tips.middle-ei: Your middle finger reaches E and I, then goes right back.
tips.pinky-p: Your right pinky reaches P, then goes back to the home row.
tips.ring-finger: Your ring finger is clever: S, L, W and the dot are its.
tips.reach-t: For the far T, stretch your index finger and return to F.
tips.feel-center: Aim for the middle of the key, even without looking.
tips.thumb-space: Press Space with the thumb that did not just type.
tips.shift-opposite: For a capital letter, press Shift with the pinky of the other hand.
tips.capital-a: You type A with the left hand, so press the right Shift.
tips.yz-swap: On a Slovak keyboard, Z is on top and Y is below.
tips.z-finger: Your right index types Z and your left pinky types Y.
tips.number-row: The number row holds ľ š č ť ž ý á í é, add Shift for digits.
tips.number-fingers: Type the top row with the same finger as the letters below it.
tips.dead-keys: Press the accent mark first, then the letter.
tips.caron-shift: The caron is the same key as the acute, with Shift.
tips.accent-pinky: The keys ú ä ô ň belong to your right pinky.
tips.diacritics-fun: Slovak accents are a little magic. You are learning it!
tips.eyes-screen: Look at the screen, your fingers will find the way.
tips.no-peeking: Tempted to peek at the keyboard? Picture the finger instead.
tips.rest-eyes: Look out the window sometimes, your eyes need rest too.
tips.accuracy-first: Be accurate first, speed will come by itself.
tips.steady-beat: Type in a steady beat, like tapping along to a song.
tips.slow-down: Making many mistakes? Slow down and it gets easier.
tips.hard-word: Type a tricky word a few times in a row, slowly at first.
tips.mistakes-ok: Mistakes are fine, you learn something from each one.
tips.patience: Feel like you're not improving? That's normal, keep going.
tips.short-sessions: A few short practices beat one long one.
tips.stretch-fingers: Spread your fingers, make fists, then open them again.
tips.stretch-wrist: Bend your wrist and gently press it with the other hand.
tips.take-break: After a few minutes, stand up, stretch and drink some water.
tips.celebrate: Great job! Your companion is proud of you too.
